job.text: Every risk assessment and incident report asks which of the three was hurt. A GRC analyst rates risks by it; a SOC analyst uses it to say how bad an incident is.

title: The CIA triad
hook: The three goals every security control serves: keep data secret, correct and available.
what: Security has three core goals, the CIA triad. Confidentiality means only the right people can see data (passwords, encryption, access control). Integrity means data is correct and hasn't been tampered with (hashes, digital signatures, change control). Availability means systems are up when people need them (backups, redundancy, DDoS protection). Almost every control you'll meet protects one or more of these, and they can pull against each other: locking something down tightly (confidentiality) can make it harder to reach (availability).

example.title: Ransomware hits all three
example.text: A ransomware attack is a neat illustration: encrypting the files destroys availability, stealing a copy first breaks confidentiality, and altering or deleting data breaks integrity. That's why it's treated as a top business risk, not just an IT problem.

source.label: NCSC: What you need to know about ransomware

defend: Confidentiality: encryption, strong authentication and least-privilege access
Integrity: hashing, digital signatures, input validation and change management
Availability: tested backups, redundancy, capacity planning and DDoS protection
Balance the three: the right level depends on what the data is worth

practice.label: Encryption & hashing lesson

checks.q: Which part of the CIA triad does encrypting a file protect?
checks.why: Encryption keeps data secret, so only someone with the key can read it. That's confidentiality.
notes: Integrity is about data being changed. Encrypting a file doesn't stop anyone editing it; think about who can read it.
Availability is about getting to the data when you need it. Encryption doesn't keep a service up.
Encryption does protect one of the three. Which one is about who can read the data?

checks.q: A website is knocked offline by a flood of traffic. Which goal has been attacked?
checks.why: If people can't reach the system when they need it, availability has failed. A DDoS attacks availability.
notes: Nothing was read by the wrong people. The site just couldn't be reached.
Nothing was changed. Think about what users couldn't do.
Authentication is about proving who you are, and it isn't one of the three goals.

checks.q: You compare a downloaded file's hash to the published one and they match. What have you confirmed?
checks.why: A matching hash shows the file is unchanged, which is integrity. (Proving who made it needs a signature.)
notes: Comparing hashes doesn't hide anything. It checks something else about the file.
A hash match doesn't keep the file reachable. It tells you whether it changed.
A hash says nothing about the author. That needs a digital signature.

checks.q: A hospital's records system is up, private and unchanged, but a fault means doctors can only open it from one ward. Which goal is weakened?
checks.why: The data is secret and correct, but the people who need it can't get to it everywhere they need it. That's availability, and in a hospital it can matter most.
notes: Nobody is reading records they shouldn't. The problem is reaching them.
The records haven't been altered. Think about access, not accuracy.
Safe data that staff can't reach when treating patients is still a security failure.

concept.why: Choose each number. Every goal of security is something real at this counter.
concept.title: The pharmacy counter: all three goals in one place

image.alt: A pharmacy counter at night. A customer shows an ID card while the pharmacist hands over a paper bag. Frosted glass hides the queue, a sealed box and a barcode scanner sit on the counter, and an OPEN sign glows above.

items.label: Frosted glass
items.text: People in the queue can't see who is collecting what, or read anything on the counter.
items.breaks: Clear glass, or reading names and medicines out loud to the queue.

items.label: The ID check
items.text: Only the right person gets the prescription: the pharmacist checks who you are before handing anything over.
items.breaks: Giving medicine to anyone who says the right name.

items.label: The sealed box
items.text: The tamper-evident seal shows nothing has been opened or swapped since the medicine left the supplier.

items.label: The barcode scan
items.text: Scanning checks this is exactly the medicine and dose on the prescription, not a lookalike.
items.breaks: Typing the code in by hand and getting one digit wrong.

items.label: Open, and handed over
items.text: The counter is open when people need it, and the right person leaves with their medicine.
items.breaks: The system crashes at five o'clock with a queue out of the door.

items.text: If the power or one computer fails, the backup unit and the second terminal keep the counter serving.

keys.label: Every control
keys.text: Almost every security control protects one of the three.

keys.label: A balancing act
keys.text: Locking data down tightly can make it harder to reach.

keys.label: Every attack
keys.text: Each breaks at least one: a leak, a change or an outage.

job.text: A GRC analyst maps the company's controls to a framework, finds the gaps before an audit, and turns them into a plan the business can fund and track.

title: Security frameworks: NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS & Cyber Essentials
hook: The playbooks organisations use to decide what to protect, and to prove they have.
what: A security framework is a tested set of good practice, so an organisation doesn't invent security from scratch. Each does a different job. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 organises a whole security programme into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, split into 22 categories. A profile describes where you are now and where you want to be. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 is the international standard for an information security management system (ISMS): a managed cycle of risk assessment, controls and review that an accredited body can certify. Its Annex A lists 93 controls in four themes: organisational, people, physical and technological. The CIS Controls v8.1 are 18 prioritised controls, broken into specific safeguards, and Implementation Group 1 is the essential starting set. In the UK, Cyber Essentials is a government-backed scheme built on five controls: firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control and malware protection. NIST SP 800-53 is the large control catalogue that US government systems use. Compliance (meeting rules like UK GDPR or PCI DSS) overlaps with security but isn't the same thing: you can be compliant and still insecure. How attackers behave (MITRE ATT&CK) is covered in How attacks are modelled.

example.title: Cyber Essentials and government contracts
example.text: Since 2014, suppliers bidding for some UK central government contracts, such as those handling personal data, have had to hold Cyber Essentials. A small firm's first framework is often the one a customer asks for.

source.label: NCSC: Cyber Essentials

defend: Choose a framework that fits your size, sector and what your customers ask for
Start with the basics: Cyber Essentials or CIS Implementation Group 1
Map one set of controls to several frameworks instead of running each separately
Treat certification as a floor: keep testing and reviewing between audits

practice.label: Would they pass Cyber Essentials?

checks.q: What are the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework?
options: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review, Repeat
Scan, Patch, Monitor, Alert, Block, Report
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Audit, Comply, Insure
checks.why: The NIST CSF groups work into Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
notes: That's the Deming cycle for improving processes, not the NIST CSF's functions.
These are security tasks, not the CSF's six functions. Govern was added in CSF 2.0.
That's the CIA triad with extra words. The CSF's functions describe stages of security work.

checks.q: Which of these can an organisation be certified against by an accredited body?
checks.why: ISO 27001 is a certifiable management system standard. The CSF and the CIS Controls are frameworks you adopt, and ATT&CK is a catalogue of attacker behaviour.
notes: The NIST CSF is a voluntary framework you adopt. No accredited body certifies against it.
ATT&CK is a catalogue of attacker techniques, not a standard you can be certified against.
The CIS Controls are a list of safeguards to adopt. There's no accredited certification for them.

checks.q: Which of these is one of Cyber Essentials' five controls?
checks.why: The five are firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control and malware protection.
notes: Cyber Essentials doesn't require a penetration test. Cyber Essentials Plus adds a hands-on check, but not a pentest.
Monitoring is good practice but isn't one of the five technical controls.
Data loss prevention isn't one of the five. They focus on basic technical hygiene.

checks.q: What is CIS Implementation Group 1?
options: The essential starting set of safeguards for any organisation
The most advanced controls, for large companies
checks.why: IG1 is 'essential cyber hygiene': the safeguards every organisation should have first. IG2 and IG3 add more for larger or higher-risk organisations.
notes: IG1 is meant for every organisation, not just governments.
CIS Implementation Groups aren't exams. They're sets of safeguards.
That's IG3. IG1 is where everyone starts.

checks.q: Which statement about compliance is true?
options: You can be compliant and still insecure
Compliance replaces the need for a framework
checks.why: Meeting rules like PCI DSS is a minimum bar; it doesn't guarantee you're actually secure.
notes: Meeting a standard sets a minimum. Attackers don't check your certificate.
Compliance applies to many businesses, like PCI DSS for anyone taking cards.
Frameworks help you organise security beyond what rules require.

checks.q: A small firm wants to bid for a government contract that requires a basic, certified security standard. Which should it get first?
checks.why: UK government contracts that handle certain data ask for Cyber Essentials: five basic controls, quick to certify. ISO 27001 is far bigger, and the others aren't certifications.
notes: ISO 27001 is certifiable but takes months and a whole management system. It's more than a basic bar.
The CSF is a framework to adopt. There's no certificate to show a buyer.
ATT&CK describes attacker behaviour. It isn't something you certify against.

concept.why: Each framework does a different job. Here is what each one is for.
concept.title: The frameworks and their jobs

items.label: NIST CSF 2.0
items.text: Organises a whole programme: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

items.label: ISO/IEC 27001
items.text: A management system you can be certified against, with 93 Annex A controls.

items.label: CIS Controls v8.1
items.text: 18 prioritised controls, broken into safeguards. Start with Implementation Group 1.

items.label: Cyber Essentials
items.text: The UK baseline: five controls, self-assessed, or audited for Plus.

items.label: NIST SP 800-53
items.text: The big control catalogue US government systems are built on.

tip: The five NIST CSF functions in order (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) spell the hook "I Previously Detected Real Risk." The newer Govern function wraps around all five.

keys.label: Don't start from scratch
keys.text: Frameworks give you tested practice to build on.

keys.label: Pick by job
keys.text: CSF organises, ISO certifies, CIS prioritises, Cyber Essentials sets a baseline.

keys.label: Compliant isn't secure
keys.text: Passing an audit doesn't mean attackers can't get in.

job.text: Audits ask which controls exist and whether they work. IT support runs many of them day to day; a SOC analyst sees which one failed during an incident.

title: Security controls
hook: Prevent, detect, correct: what each defence is for.
what: A control is anything that reduces risk. Controls come in four categories by how they work: technical (enforced by technology, like a firewall or MFA), managerial (decisions and policies, like a risk assessment), operational (things people do, like security awareness training or checking logs) and physical (locks, fences, badges). Each control also has a type, by what it does: preventive controls stop something happening, deterrent controls discourage the attempt, detective controls notice it, corrective controls fix things afterwards, directive controls tell people what to do, and compensating controls stand in when the usual control can't be used. Good defence layers several types, because no single control is perfect.

example.title: Target
example.text: Attackers got in using a heating contractor's stolen login and planted malware on Target's checkout tills, taking about 40 million payment card numbers. Bloomberg Businessweek later reported that Target's malware detection system had raised alerts during the attack and nobody acted on them. A detective control did its job; there was no response to correct the problem.

source.label: Infosecurity Magazine: Target may have ignored pre-breach intrusion warning

defend: Pair every detective control with someone who acts on its alerts
Layer controls so one failure isn't the whole defence
Add a compensating control when a system can't meet the standard, and write down why
Review controls after incidents: which one should have stopped this?

practice.label: Practise control types in the Security+ questions

checks.q: An intrusion detection system alerts the SOC but lets the traffic through. What type of control is it?
checks.why: It notices and reports. A prevention system (IPS) would block the traffic.
notes: A preventive control would stop the traffic. This one lets it through.
Corrective controls fix things afterwards, like restoring from backup.
Directive controls tell people what to do, like a policy.

checks.q: Which category does a written acceptable use policy belong to?
checks.why: Policies are decisions set by management. Corrective is a type, not a category.
notes: Technical controls are enforced by technology. A policy is written down by management.
Physical controls are things like locks and fences.
Corrective is a type of control (what it does), not a category (what it is).

checks.q: What does the Target breach show about detective controls?
options: They only work with someone ready to act on the alerts
They should be switched off to reduce noise
checks.why: The alerts were raised; the missing piece was a response to them.
notes: The alerts did fire. They were useful; nobody acted.
Detection can't replace prevention. They work together.
Turning alerts off would hide attacks. Tuning, not switching off, reduces noise.

concept.why: Choose each number. One office entrance holds all six types of control.
concept.title: An office entrance at night: six controls, six jobs

image.alt: An office entrance at night. A keycard reader beside a glass door with a camera sticker, a CCTV camera on the wall, a framed policy, and a guard at a desk with a sign-in book, a pen and a backup drive.

items.label: Keycard reader
items.text: Stops it happening: no valid card, no way in.
items.breaks: The door wedged open for a delivery.

items.label: Camera sticker
items.text: Puts people off trying: they know they're being watched.
items.breaks: A sticker with no camera behind it, once people work that out.

items.label: CCTV camera
items.text: Doesn't stop anyone, but records who came and went, so you can spot and investigate it.
items.breaks: Nobody reviews the footage, or it records over itself after a day.

items.label: Backup drive
items.text: Fixes things afterwards: restore the files an attacker deleted or encrypted.
items.breaks: A backup that's always plugged in, so ransomware encrypts it too.

items.label: The framed policy
items.text: Tells people what to do: wear your badge, don't hold the door for strangers.
items.breaks: A policy nobody has read or is held to.

items.label: Sign-in book and guard
items.text: Stands in when the usual control can't be used: if the reader breaks, the guard checks ID and signs visitors in by hand.
items.breaks: Signing in anyone without checking who they are.

keys.text: How it works: technical, managerial, operational or physical.

keys.label: Types

job.text: Reported emails land in the SOC queue every day: check the headers and links, find who else got it, and pull it from every mailbox. IT support takes the first 'I clicked it' call.

explainer.why: A stolen password is rarely the end of it. Once inside a mailbox, an attacker adds a hidden rule to bury the replies that would expose the fraud. Toggle it below.

title: Phishing & social engineering
hook: Phishing is one of the three most common ways attackers get in, and it targets people, not machines.
what: Phishing is tricking someone into clicking a link, opening a file, handing over a password or sending money by pretending to be someone they trust. Social engineering is the wider skill of manipulating people: fake IT support calls (vishing), texts (smishing), or emails that impersonate the boss asking for an urgent payment (business email compromise). Attackers lean on urgency, authority and fear because people under pressure skip the checks they'd normally do.

example.title: MGM Resorts (Scattered Spider)
example.text: Attackers reportedly found an employee on LinkedIn, called the IT help desk pretending to be them, and talked staff into resetting their login. That one phone call led to ransomware that shut down hotel systems and cost MGM about $100 million, by its own filing.

source.label: MGM Resorts 8-K filing, SEC (October 2023)

defend: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys or security keys) so a stolen password isn't enough
Verify unusual requests through a second channel you already trust
Make reporting easy and never punish people for clicking
Email filtering plus SPF, DKIM and DMARC to block spoofed senders

practice.label: Take Google's phishing quiz

checks.q: Your 'CEO' emails asking you to buy gift cards urgently and keep it quiet. What's the best move?
options: Buy them quickly, it's the CEO
Reply to the email to ask if it's real
Contact the CEO through a known phone number or chat
Forward it to colleagues to see what they think
checks.why: Replying goes straight back to the attacker. Verify through a channel you already trust.
notes: Urgency and secrecy are the trick. A real CEO can wait for you to check.
Replying goes straight back to whoever sent it, so of course it'll say it's real.
Forwarding spreads a phishing email further. Verify with the sender first.

checks.q: An email says your account will be closed within the hour unless you sign in now. Which trick is it mainly relying on?
checks.why: Attackers lean on urgency, authority and fear because people under pressure skip the checks they'd normally do.
notes: Credential stuffing uses passwords leaked elsewhere. This email is pushing you to act now.
Nothing in the email is about encryption. Think about the pressure it creates.
A zero-day is an unpatched flaw. This trick works on people, not software.

checks.q: You typed your password into a fake login page. Which defence still stops the attacker getting in?
options: Phishing-resistant MFA such as a passkey or security key
checks.why: A passkey or security key only works on the real website, so a stolen password on its own isn't enough.
notes: The attacker already has the password, however long it is.
Clearing history doesn't take back the password you typed.
Antivirus on your phone doesn't stop someone signing in with your password elsewhere.

diagram.why: Step through a phishing attack from the first email to the stolen login, so you can see where it is stopped.
diagram.title: How a credential-phishing attack unfolds

steps.msg: Email: “Your mailbox is full. Sign in to keep it.”
steps.text: The email looks like it comes from IT and adds urgency so the reader acts before thinking.
steps.stop: Email filtering and SPF, DKIM and DMARC catch many spoofed senders.

stage.body:
Hello Alex,

Your mailbox has reached its limit and will stop receiving mail within the hour.

Sign in to raise the limit and keep your mail.

IT Support

link.text: Sign in to keep your mail

steps.msg: Clicks the link and types a password
steps.text: The link opens a copy of the real sign-in page on a lookalike address.
steps.stop: Check the address; report it. Never punish people who click.

steps.text: Whatever is typed into the fake page goes straight to the attacker.
With the password, the attacker logs in to the real account to read mail or phish colleagues from a trusted address.
steps.stop: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys) blocks this step: the password alone isn't enough.

stage.subject: Q4 numbers for Friday
stage.body:
Alex,

The Q4 pack is in the shared drive. Can you send the board version before Friday?

Priya

keys.label: The bait
keys.text: A message pretending to be someone you trust.

keys.label: The pressure
keys.text: Urgency, authority and fear make people skip checks.

keys.label: The prize
keys.text: A click, a file opened, a password or a payment.

job.text: A SOC analyst spots the early signs (odd admin logins, backups deleted) and isolates machines; IT support rebuilds them and restores from the backups they keep tested.

title: Ransomware
hook: Encrypt everything, steal a copy, then demand payment twice.
what: Ransomware is malware that encrypts an organisation's files so they can't be used, then demands payment for the key. Modern gangs also steal the data first and threaten to publish it (double extortion). Most groups run as businesses: developers rent the ransomware to 'affiliates' who break in, often through stolen passwords, unpatched VPNs or phishing, then spend days quietly spreading before they strike.

example.title: Colonial Pipeline
example.text: Attackers logged in to an old VPN account with a leaked password and no MFA. The resulting ransomware attack shut down the largest fuel pipeline in the US for days and caused fuel shortages along the East Coast.

source.label: CISA: The attack on Colonial Pipeline

defend: Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly
MFA on every remote access point (VPN, RDP, email)
Patch internet-facing systems first, especially anything on CISA's KEV list
Endpoint detection (EDR) and watching for mass file changes

practice.label: See free decryptors at No More Ransom

checks.q: Why aren't backups alone enough against modern ransomware?
options: Gangs also steal data and threaten to leak it
checks.why: Double extortion means restoring from backup doesn't stop the leak threat.
notes: Good backups aren't encrypted by the attacker if they're kept offline. The problem is what else gangs do.
Restoring your own backups is perfectly legal.
Ransomware doesn't remove the internet. Think about the stolen data.

checks.q: In ransomware-as-a-service, who usually breaks into the victim's network?
checks.why: Developers rent the ransomware to affiliates, who break in, often with stolen passwords or unpatched VPNs, and spread before striking.
notes: Developers write and rent out the ransomware. Someone else does the breaking in.
Antivirus vendors defend against it.
The IT team is the victim here, not the attacker.

checks.q: Which backups are most likely to survive a ransomware attack?
options: A copy on the same server
Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly
Backups on a mapped network drive
checks.why: Gangs hunt for reachable backups and destroy them. Offline or immutable copies can't be changed, and testing proves they actually restore.
notes: The Recycle Bin is on the same disk and is easily emptied.
A copy on the same server is encrypted along with everything else.
Ransomware encrypts anything it can reach, including mapped drives.

checks.q: At 02:00 your EDR shows a server deleting its shadow copies with vssadmin. What do you do first?
options: Isolate the server from the network and alert the incident lead
Reboot it to clear the problem
Wait to see if files start being renamed
Email all staff to stop working
checks.why: Deleting shadow copies is a classic step just before encryption. Isolating stops the spread while keeping the machine on for evidence, and the incident lead starts the response.
notes: A reboot can destroy evidence in memory and may let the encryption finish. Contain it first.
Waiting gives the attacker time to encrypt. Deleting backups is already the warning sign.
Emailing everyone is slow and may tip off an attacker reading mail. Contain the server first.

explainer.why: Step through an attack from the first login to encryption, then pick two defences and see where it stops.

keys.label: Encrypt
keys.text: Files are scrambled until a ransom is paid.

keys.label: Steal first
keys.text: A copy is taken and leaked if you don't pay.

keys.label: A business
keys.text: Developers rent it to affiliates who break in.

job.text: A SOC analyst reads the EDR alert and process tree, decides whether it ran and what it touched, isolates the machine, and checks the rest of the estate for the same file.

title: Malware families
hook: Trojans, worms, stealers, RATs: know what you're looking at.
what: Malware is any software built to cause harm. A trojan pretends to be something useful. A worm spreads by itself between machines. An infostealer grabs saved passwords, cookies and crypto wallets. A RAT (remote access trojan) gives the attacker control of your machine. A loader's only job is to download other malware. A botnet is thousands of infected devices taking orders from one controller.

example.title: WannaCry
example.text: A ransomware worm used a leaked NSA exploit (EternalBlue) to spread across unpatched Windows machines worldwide in hours, hitting the UK's NHS hard. Microsoft had released the patch two months earlier.

source.label: National Audit Office: Investigation into WannaCry and the NHS

defend: Keep systems patched so worms have nowhere to spread
Only install software from trusted sources
Use EDR and application allow-listing
Don't let browsers store high-value passwords on shared machines

practice.label: Look up a file hash on VirusTotal

checks.q: Which malware type steals saved browser passwords and session cookies?
checks.why: Infostealers are a big driver of account takeovers because stolen cookies can bypass MFA.
notes: A worm spreads itself between machines. Think about which type is after saved logins.
A loader only fetches more malware.
Adware shows unwanted adverts; it doesn't steal passwords.

checks.q: Which type of malware spreads between machines by itself, without anyone clicking anything?
checks.why: A worm spreads on its own, which is why keeping systems patched (leaving it nothing to exploit) matters so much.
notes: A loader downloads other malware, but someone has to run it.
A trojan pretends to be something useful, so someone has to open it.
An infostealer steals data from the machine it's on; it doesn't spread.

checks.q: A program's only job is to download and run other malware. What is it?
checks.why: A loader fetches the next stage. Blocking it stops everything that would have followed.
notes: A RAT gives an attacker remote control.
Adware shows adverts.
A botnet is many infected machines controlled together, not a single downloader.

checks.q: A user opened an 'invoice' and their browser's saved passwords were sent out. Resetting their Windows password is done. What else must happen?
options: Sign them out everywhere and reset the passwords saved in the browser
Nothing more: the Windows password is changed
Delete the invoice from their Downloads folder
Run a full antivirus scan and close the ticket
checks.why: An infostealer takes saved passwords and session cookies. Stolen sessions work without the password, so they must be ended, and every saved password changed from a clean device.
notes: The stolen data is browser passwords and cookies, not the Windows login.
Deleting the file doesn't undo what it already sent.
A scan can't take back stolen sessions; they still work until they're ended.

scene.title: One desk, three ways in

image.alt: Someone at a desk at night reaches for a plain USB stick. Their laptop shows an email with an attachment, and a backup drive is plugged in beside it.

items.label: A USB stick of unknown origin
items.text: Found or handed over, it can carry malware that runs when it's plugged in, or even pretend to be a keyboard.
items.fix: Don't plug in unknown drives: hand them to IT. Block or scan USB storage on work machines.

items.label: An unexpected attachment
items.text: Most malware still arrives by email: an 'invoice' or 'document' that runs code when it's opened.
items.fix: Check the sender and the file type, open nothing you weren't expecting, and report it.

items.label: A backup drive left plugged in
items.text: Ransomware encrypts every drive it can reach, including a backup that's always connected.
items.fix: Keep at least one backup offline or unchangeable, and test that you can restore from it.

concept.why: Malware is grouped by what it does. Here are the main families and how each behaves.
concept.title: The main families

items.label: Virus
items.text: Attaches to a file or program and spreads when that file is run by a person.

items.label: Worm
items.text: Spreads by itself across a network, with no user action, exploiting weaknesses.

items.label: Trojan
items.text: Disguised as something useful; the user installs it believing it's safe.

items.label: Ransomware
items.text: Encrypts files and demands payment; often steals a copy first to add pressure.

items.label: Spyware / infostealer
items.text: Quietly harvests passwords, cookies and keystrokes and sends them to the attacker.

items.label: Rootkit
items.text: Hides deep in the system to stay invisible and keep access across reboots.

items.label: Botnet
items.text: Many infected machines controlled together, rented out for spam or DDoS.

items.label: RAT
items.text: A remote-access trojan gives the attacker a hands-on backdoor into the machine.

keys.label: Trojans and worms
keys.text: One pretends to be useful; one spreads by itself.

keys.label: Infostealers
keys.text: Grab saved passwords, cookies and crypto wallets.

keys.label: RATs and botnets
keys.text: Remote control of one machine, or of thousands.

job.text: When a vendor warns of an exploited flaw with no patch, the team applies the workaround the same day, hunts for signs it was already used, and patches the moment the fix lands.

title: Zero-days
hook: A bug the vendor has had zero days to fix.
what: A zero-day is a vulnerability attackers know about before the vendor does, so there's no patch yet. When it's being used in real attacks it's an 'in-the-wild zero-day'. They're rare and valuable, often used by nation-states or spyware vendors. Once a patch ships, it becomes an 'n-day', and the race is on: attackers reverse-engineer the patch while defenders try to install it.

example.title: Log4Shell
example.text: A flaw in Log4j, a logging library inside thousands of Java apps, let attackers run code just by getting a server to log a crafted string. It was exploited within hours of going public, and teams spent weeks just finding where Log4j was hiding.

source.label: CISA: Apache Log4j vulnerability guidance

defend: Know what software you run (an asset inventory and SBOM)
Layered defences so one bug isn't game over
Apply vendor mitigations quickly, before a patch exists
Monitor for unusual behaviour, not only known signatures

practice.label: Browse Google Project Zero's in-the-wild tracker

checks.q: When does a zero-day stop being a zero-day?
options: When the vendor releases a patch
When it gets a CVSS score
checks.why: Once a fix exists it's an n-day, but unpatched systems are still vulnerable.
notes: There's no time limit. The name is about whether a fix exists.
A score says how bad it could be, not whether it's fixed.
It does stop. Think about what the vendor eventually releases.

checks.q: What is an 'n-day'?
options: A bug nobody has found yet
A vulnerability with no CVE ID
A known vulnerability that already has a patch
checks.why: Once a patch ships, a zero-day becomes an n-day: attackers study the patch while defenders race to install it.
notes: That's a zero-day nobody has discovered. 'n-day' means it's known.
Not having a CVE ID doesn't make something an n-day.
Who found it doesn't matter. It's about whether a patch exists.

checks.q: There's no patch yet for a zero-day in software you run. What helps most right now?
options: Apply the vendor's mitigations and watch for unusual behaviour
checks.why: Vendors often publish workarounds before a fix, and behaviour monitoring catches attacks that signatures miss.
notes: The Wi-Fi password has nothing to do with a flaw in your software.
Removing everything stops the business working. There are targeted steps.
Doing nothing leaves you exposed while attackers are already using it.

concept.why: A flaw moves from hidden to patched. Here is its life, and what defenders can do at each stage.
concept.title: The life of a flaw

items.label: Zero-day
items.text: A flaw the vendor doesn't know about yet: zero days to fix it. No patch exists.

items.label: In the wild
items.text: Attackers exploit it quietly before anyone defends against it. The most dangerous window.

items.label: Patch released
items.text: The vendor ships a fix once they learn of it. The race to install it begins.

items.label: N-day
items.text: After disclosure the flaw is public; unpatched systems are easy targets for everyone.

keys.label: No patch yet
keys.text: Attackers know about the bug before the vendor does.

keys.label: Rare and valuable
keys.text: Often used by nation-states and spyware vendors.

keys.label: Then a race
keys.text: Once patched, attackers and defenders both rush.

explainer.why: Drag when you patch. The zero-day window is out of your hands; the window after the fix is out is yours.

job.text: Every week someone reads the scan results, drops the false positives, ranks what's left by exposure and exploitation, and chases the fixes through change management.

title: Vulnerabilities & patching
hook: CVE, CVSS, EPSS, KEV: how teams decide what to fix first.
what: Every public security bug gets a CVE ID. CVSS scores how bad it could be (0–10). EPSS estimates how likely it is to be exploited in the next 30 days. CISA's KEV list confirms which are being exploited right now. Tens of thousands of CVEs appear every year, far more than anyone can patch at once, so good teams prioritise by real-world risk: exploited first, likely next, then severity.

example.title: Equifax
example.text: A patch for a critical Apache Struts flaw was available for two months, but one internet-facing system wasn't updated. Attackers used it to steal personal data on about 147 million people.

source.label: US GAO report GAO-18-559 on the Equifax breach

defend: Keep an accurate inventory of systems and software
Patch KEV-listed and internet-facing issues first
Use EPSS alongside CVSS to cut the noise
Track time-to-patch as a team metric

practice.label: Explore this week's CVEs on the Radar

checks.q: A CVE has CVSS 6.5 and is on CISA's KEV list. Another has CVSS 9.8 with EPSS 0.2%. Which should most teams patch first?
options: The 6.5 on KEV, because it's being exploited
checks.why: Confirmed exploitation beats a theoretical worst case.
notes: A high score is a worst case. The other is being exploited right now.
Both already have patches. Waiting helps attackers.
Publication date doesn't tell you which is more dangerous.

checks.q: What does EPSS estimate?
options: How severe a vulnerability could be
How likely a vulnerability is to be exploited in the next 30 days
How long a patch takes to install
checks.why: CVSS scores how bad a bug could be; EPSS estimates the chance it's exploited in the next 30 days.
notes: That's CVSS: how bad it could be.
EPSS doesn't count affected machines; your own inventory tells you that.
It says nothing about how long a patch takes.

checks.q: What does a CVE ID give you?
options: A unique name for one public vulnerability
checks.why: A CVE ID is a shared name so everyone means the same bug. Severity comes from CVSS, and exploitation from CISA's KEV list.
notes: A CVE ID names a bug; it doesn't fix it.
Exploitation evidence comes from lists like KEV, not the CVE ID.
Severity comes from CVSS, a separate score.

concept.why: Patching is a loop, not a one-off. Here are the stages it runs through.
concept.title: The patching loop

items.label: Identify
items.text: Scan and inventory. You can't fix what you don't know you have.

items.label: Prioritise
items.text: Rank by real risk (what's exploited now (KEV), exposed, and critical) not just raw severity.

items.label: Remediate
items.text: Patch, configure around it, or isolate it. Then move to the next most dangerous.

items.label: Verify
items.text: Re-scan to confirm the fix took, and feed what you learned back into the next round.

keys.label: CVE
keys.text: An ID for every public security bug.

keys.label: CVSS and EPSS
keys.text: How bad it could be, and how likely it's exploited.

keys.label: KEV
keys.text: Bugs confirmed as being exploited right now. Fix these first.

job.text: A cloud engineer pins and reviews dependencies and locks down build secrets; a GRC analyst assesses suppliers and writes what they must report into their contracts.

title: Supply chain attacks
hook: Why break in when you can ship inside a trusted update?
what: A supply chain attack compromises something many organisations trust (a software vendor, an update server, an open-source package or a managed service provider) so the attacker reaches all of their customers at once. Malicious npm and PyPI packages, typosquatted library names and hijacked maintainer accounts are now constant.

example.title: XZ Utils backdoor
example.text: Over two years, an attacker built trust as a helpful maintainer of a compression library used by Linux, then slipped in a backdoor targeting SSH. A Microsoft engineer spotted it because SSH logins were half a second slower than usual.

source.label: The original disclosure on oss-security (Andres Freund)

defend: Pin and verify dependencies; review what new packages do
Generate SBOMs so you can answer 'are we affected?' fast
Limit what build systems and vendors can access
Check signatures and provenance (frameworks like SLSA)

practice.label: Read the SLSA supply-chain framework

checks.q: What made the XZ Utils attack so dangerous?
options: It used a zero-click iPhone bug
A trusted maintainer inserted the backdoor
checks.why: Trust was the attack vector. Code review and reproducible builds are key defences.
notes: That describes Pegasus-style spyware. XZ Utils was about trust in a maintainer.
It didn't arrive by email. It was hidden inside trusted open-source code.
XZ Utils is a Linux compression library.

checks.q: Why do attackers target software vendors and open-source packages?
options: One compromise reaches every organisation that trusts them
They're easier to find on the internet
checks.why: Compromising something many organisations trust lets an attacker reach all of its customers at once.
notes: Attacking vendors is just as illegal. Think about reach.
Vendors use passwords like anyone else. The draw is how many customers trust them.
Being findable isn't the reason. It's what one breach unlocks.

checks.q: What is typosquatting in package registries?
options: Publishing a malicious package named like a popular one
checks.why: Attackers publish packages with names one typo away from popular libraries, hoping a developer installs theirs by mistake.
notes: Encryption has nothing to do with it. Look at the package names.
It's not about typing speed; it's about catching a typing mistake.
CVE IDs aren't involved. The trick is in package names.

checks.q: A pull request adds a package called 'reqeusts', published two days ago with 30 downloads. What do you do?
options: Reject it and check whether the build already ran its install script
Rename it to 'requests' in the file and merge
Ask the author if it's safe
checks.why: A brand-new package one typo from a famous one is a classic typosquat. Its install script may already have run in CI, so check what the build exposed and rotate any secrets.
notes: Tests check the app works, not whether a dependency stole something.
Fixing the name stops future installs but ignores what the bad one may already have done.
The PR author may simply have made a typo. Check the package and the build yourself.

scene.why: Choose each number. Each of these is trusted because of who it came from.
scene.title: The contractor's visit: trusted, and unchecked

image.alt: A server room at night. A contractor plugs their own laptop into a network socket on the wall. An unopened parcel and a USB stick sit on the desk, a monitor shows an update installing, and a staff member by the door looks at their phone.

items.label: The contractor's own laptop
items.text: A supplier's laptop plugged straight into the network brings whatever is on it inside your defences.
items.fix: Give visitors a separate, isolated network, or a managed laptop you supply.

items.label: An unexpected delivery
items.text: Equipment can be tampered with before it arrives. An unrequested parcel in the server room is a question, not a gift.
items.fix: Check deliveries against orders, and inspect seals before anything is installed.

items.label: A USB stick from the supplier
items.text: Drivers or firmware 'on a stick' are a classic way in.
items.fix: Download updates from the vendor's official site and check they're signed.

items.label: An update installing
items.text: Updates are trusted by design, so an attacker who poisons a vendor's update reaches every customer at once, as in the SolarWinds attack of 2020.
items.fix: Roll updates out to a small group first, and watch what updated software does on the network.

items.label: Nobody watching
items.text: The staff member is on their phone, so nobody sees what the contractor plugs in or copies.
items.fix: Escort third parties in sensitive rooms, and log what they connect.

concept.why: You rely on a lot of code you did not write. Here is where that trust gets abused.
concept.title: Where the trust is abused

items.label: Vendor updates
items.text: A trusted software update is laced with malware, so every customer installs it (SolarWinds).

items.label: Dependencies
items.text: A popular open-source package is poisoned; every project that pulls it in is affected.

items.label: Build pipeline
items.text: Attackers compromise the build system so malicious code is signed and shipped as genuine.

items.label: Third-party access
items.text: A supplier or MSP with a login into your network becomes the way in.

keys.label: Hit the supplier
keys.text: Compromise one vendor, update or package that many trust.

keys.label: Reach everyone
keys.text: Every customer installs the attacker's code themselves.

keys.label: Packages
keys.text: Malicious and typosquatted npm and PyPI packages are constant.

job.text: A SOC analyst works out what left and when; a GRC analyst decides with the data protection lead whether to tell the ICO and the people affected, inside 72 hours.

title: Data breaches
hook: Your data is probably already out there. Here's what that means.
what: A data breach is when information is accessed or taken by someone who shouldn't have it. It can be a hack, a misconfigured database left open to the internet, or an insider. Stolen data is sold, leaked or used for further attacks. Reused passwords from one breach get tried on other sites, which is called credential stuffing.

example.title: MOVEit
example.text: The Cl0p gang used a SQL injection zero-day in MOVEit Transfer, a file-sharing product, to steal data from over 2,700 organisations in one campaign, exposing personal data on roughly 93 million people.

source.label: CISA and FBI advisory AA23-158A: CL0P exploits MOVEit

defend: Collect and keep less data
Encrypt sensitive data and lock down database exposure
Unique passwords and a password manager for everyone
Monitor for leaked company credentials

practice.label: Check your email on Have I Been Pwned

checks.q: What is credential stuffing?
options: Guessing passwords one letter at a time
Trying leaked username/password pairs on other sites
Putting too many passwords in a manager
checks.why: It works because people reuse passwords. Unique passwords stop it.
notes: That's brute force. Credential stuffing reuses real leaked pairs.
Password managers are a defence, not the attack.
Attackers don't need to encrypt stolen passwords to use them.

checks.q: Which of these is a data breach?
options: A stranger downloads a customer database that was left open to the internet
A website goes offline for an hour
checks.why: A breach is any access to data by someone who shouldn't have it. Misconfigured, exposed databases count, not only hacks.
notes: Installing an update is normal maintenance.
A slow network is a performance problem, not a breach.
An outage hits availability, but no data reached the wrong people.

checks.q: What stops credential stuffing from working on your accounts?
options: A different password for every site, kept in a password manager
checks.why: Credential stuffing replays passwords leaked from one site on others, so it only works when a password is reused.
notes: One strong password reused everywhere is exactly what stuffing exploits.
Cookies don't matter here; the attacker logs in with the password itself.
Attackers usually use your email address, which you can't easily change.

checks.q: You find a test database with real customer emails was public for a week. Logs show one unknown download. What comes first?
options: Close the access, keep the logs and tell whoever handles breach reporting
Delete the database so nobody can find it
Wait until you know who downloaded it
Email the customers straight away yourself
checks.why: Stop the exposure, preserve evidence and hand it to the people who decide on reporting. In the UK the 72-hour clock starts when the organisation becomes aware.
notes: Deleting it destroys the evidence of what was exposed.
You may never know who it was, and the reporting clock is already running.
Telling customers is decided by the people responsible for breaches, with the facts in hand.

scene.why: Choose each number. Most breaches start with something small left open, like these.
scene.title: An office after hours: four ways data walks out

image.alt: An office at night. A monitor left unlocked showing a spreadsheet, a sticky note on its edge, printouts left in a printer, a window propped open, and a cleaner walking away in the background.

items.label: An unlocked screen
items.text: Anyone walking past can read the customer spreadsheet, copy it, or use the account that's still signed in.
items.fix: Lock the screen (Windows key + L) whenever you step away, and set it to lock itself after a few minutes.

items.label: A password on a sticky note
items.text: A password in plain sight: a visitor, a cleaner or a photo taken in the office can capture it.
items.fix: Use a password manager, and multi-factor authentication so a password alone isn't enough.

items.label: Printouts in the tray
items.text: Printed customer details left overnight can leave the building without anyone noticing.
items.fix: Use secure print release (it prints only when you're at the printer), and shred what you don't need.

items.label: A window left open
items.text: An open window is a way in that skips every door lock and badge reader.
items.fix: Close and lock windows at the end of the day, and check them on the last walk-round.

items.label: Out-of-hours access
items.text: Cleaners and contractors work here at night. Most are honest, but everything left out is on show.
items.fix: A clear-desk policy: lock papers away and lock screens before you leave.

concept.why: Most breaches begin in a few familiar ways. Here they are before we go deeper.
concept.title: How breaches usually start

items.label: Stolen credentials
items.text: Reused or phished passwords let attackers log in as a real user. It's the most common route.

items.label: Misconfiguration
items.text: An exposed database or storage bucket left open to the internet with no password.

items.label: Unpatched flaw
items.text: A known vulnerability that was never fixed gives attackers a way in.

items.label: Phishing
items.text: A convincing email tricks someone into handing over access or running malware.

items.label: Insider
items.text: A careless or malicious employee leaks or takes data they can already reach.

keys.label: Data gets out
keys.text: Through a hack, an open database or an insider.

keys.label: Then it's used
keys.text: Sold, leaked or used for the next attack.

keys.label: Reused passwords
keys.text: One breach's passwords get tried everywhere else.

job.text: Analysts read joint advisories, turn their indicators and techniques into searches, and hunt their own logs for quiet, patient visitors that antivirus won't flag.

title: Nation-state hackers (APTs)
hook: Patient, well-funded and usually after secrets, not ransom.
what: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are hacking groups backed by governments. They spy, steal intellectual property, pre-position inside critical infrastructure and sometimes sabotage. Security companies give them names (Fancy Bear, Lazarus, Volt Typhoon) and track their tactics. Many 'live off the land', using built-in admin tools so they blend in with normal activity.

example.title: SolarWinds
example.text: Russian intelligence hackers slipped a backdoor into updates for SolarWinds Orion, network software used by about 18,000 organisations, then picked high-value targets including US government agencies.

source.label: CISA Emergency Directive 21-01: SolarWinds Orion

defend: Map defences to attacker behaviour using MITRE ATT&CK
Log and review use of admin tools like PowerShell
Segment networks so one foothold doesn't reach everything
Threat hunting: assume breach and look for it

practice.label: Browse threat groups on MITRE ATT&CK

checks.q: What does 'living off the land' mean?
options: Using a system's own legitimate tools to avoid detection
checks.why: Built-in tools look normal, so defenders watch how they're used, not just whether they run.
notes: It has nothing to do with location. Look at which tools are used.
It's not about farming. Think about the tools already on the system.
It's used on ordinary computers, not just physical infrastructure.

checks.q: What does APT stand for?
checks.why: APTs are government-backed groups that spy, steal and pre-position, often staying hidden for a long time.
notes: APTs use phishing, but that's not what the letters mean.
Not related to piracy.
Penetration testers are authorised. An APT is the threat itself.

checks.q: Which framework maps attacker tactics so defenders can check what they'd detect?
checks.why: MITRE ATT&CK catalogues how attackers behave, so teams can map their defences and find the gaps.
notes: CVSS scores how severe a vulnerability is.
GDPR is a data protection law.
TLS encrypts connections.

checks.q: A joint advisory says a state-backed group uses ntdsutil and netsh to stay hidden. How should your SOC respond?
options: Search your logs for those tools run by unusual accounts or at odd times
Block every Windows admin tool on every machine
Ignore it: you're not a government target
checks.why: Living off the land leaves no malware for antivirus. Hunt for unusual use of normal tools and check who ran them.
notes: Admins need these tools. Look for unusual use, not all use.
These tools are legitimate, so antivirus won't flag them.
These groups also target suppliers and critical services. The advisory exists to be checked against.

concept.why: A state-backed attacker behaves unlike a smash-and-grab. Here is what sets one apart.
concept.title: What makes an APT different

items.label: Well-resourced
items.text: Government backing means money, skilled teams and time ordinary criminals don't have.

items.label: Patient
items.text: They stay hidden for months or years (long dwell time), watching and waiting.

items.label: Custom tools
items.text: Bespoke malware and zero-days built for one target, hard to detect with signatures.

items.label: Chosen targets
items.text: Espionage, sabotage or influence against specific governments, firms or infrastructure.

keys.label: Government-backed
keys.text: Groups called APTs, with time and money.

keys.label: After secrets
keys.text: Spying, stealing ideas and hiding inside infrastructure.

keys.label: Hard to spot
keys.text: They use built-in admin tools to blend in.

job.text: The team tells a real flood from a busy day, calls the provider or scrubbing service for floods that fill the link, and rate-limits the ones aimed at the app.

title: DDoS attacks
hook: Knock a site offline by drowning it in traffic.

explainer.why: You have met the attack. Now watch what a flood does to a server as the requests pile up, and why it is hard to tell from a genuinely busy day.

what: A Distributed Denial of Service attack floods a website or network with so much traffic from so many machines that real users can't get through. The traffic usually comes from botnets of hacked computers, routers and cameras. DDoS is used for extortion, activism (hacktivism), or as a distraction during another attack.

example.title: Mirai and Dyn
example.text: The Mirai botnet infected hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers that still used factory-default passwords, then hit DNS provider Dyn, making Twitter, Netflix, Reddit and others unreachable for parts of a day.

source.label: US Department of Justice: Mirai botnet guilty pleas

defend: DDoS protection from a CDN or cloud provider
Rate limiting and caching
Change default passwords on every device
A plan for who to call when it happens

practice.label: Cloudflare's DDoS explainer

checks.q: How did Mirai build such a big botnet?
checks.why: It simply tried a short list of default usernames and passwords.
notes: Mirai didn't need a Windows bug. Think about the devices it took over.
No email was involved; it scanned the internet for devices.
It didn't pay for servers. It used devices people had left with factory logins.

checks.q: What does 'distributed' mean in DDoS?
options: The traffic comes from many machines at once
It attacks many websites at once
checks.why: The flood comes from many machines, usually a botnet, which is why blocking one source doesn't stop it.
notes: It isn't about databases. Think about where the traffic comes from.
One DDoS usually hits one target. The 'distributed' part is about the sources.
Worms spread themselves. A DDoS is about the flood's sources.

checks.q: Which defence helps most against a large DDoS attack?
options: DDoS protection from a CDN or cloud provider
checks.why: Big providers absorb floods across their global networks before the traffic ever reaches you.
notes: HTTPS doesn't make a flood worse, and turning it off exposes users.
A password doesn't stop traffic arriving.
Antivirus doesn't stop a flood of requests.

checks.q: Your shop's site slows to a crawl just as a big sale starts. Traffic is normal web requests from thousands of real customers. What is it?
options: A flash crowd: real demand, so add capacity or a queue
A DDoS: block the busiest addresses
checks.why: Normal requests at a predictable moment from real customers are demand, not an attack. Blocking them turns paying customers away.
notes: Blocking busy addresses blocks customers, including shared mobile networks.
Nothing points to an unpatched flaw. Look at the timing and the traffic.
The firewall is passing normal traffic. The servers are simply busy.

concept.why: Floods come in different shapes. Here is how each overwhelms a target.
concept.title: The shapes a flood takes

items.label: Volumetric
items.text: Raw bandwidth: fill the pipe with so much traffic nothing else gets through.

items.label: Protocol
items.text: Abuse how connections are set up, like a SYN flood exhausting the server's queue.

items.label: Application-layer
items.text: Cheap-looking requests that are expensive to answer, exhausting the app itself.

items.label: Amplification
items.text: Bounce small spoofed requests off open servers so huge replies hit the victim.

keys.label: Many machines
keys.text: Botnets of hacked computers, routers and cameras.

keys.label: One target
keys.text: So much traffic that real users can't get through.

keys.label: Why
keys.text: Extortion, protest, or a distraction from another attack.

job.text: Engineers keep AI tools to the least access they need and block ways out for data; GRC writes the rules for what staff may paste into them.

title: AI & security
hook: Deepfakes, prompt injection and AI-powered defence.
what: AI cuts both ways. Attackers use it to write convincing phishing in any language, clone voices and faces for fraud, and speed up finding bugs. AI systems also bring new weaknesses: prompt injection hides instructions in content an AI reads so it does something its user didn't intend, and AI agents with access to tools can be tricked into leaking data. Defenders use AI to sort alerts, analyse malware and spot anomalies faster.

example.title: Arup deepfake call
example.text: An employee at engineering firm Arup joined a video call with what looked like the CFO and colleagues, all of them deepfakes, and was talked into sending about $25 million to criminals.

source.label: CNN Business via ABC17: Arup revealed as $25 million deepfake scam victim

defend: Verify payment requests out-of-band, even on video
Treat anything an AI reads (web pages, emails, files) as untrusted
Give AI agents the least access they need and require approval for risky actions
Follow the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications

practice.label: Try to trick an AI in Gandalf

checks.q: What is prompt injection?
options: Hiding instructions in content an AI processes to hijack its behaviour
Training an AI on bad data
checks.why: The AI can't reliably tell its user's instructions from text it's reading.
notes: Length isn't the problem. It's what's hidden in the content.
SQL injection targets databases. This is about instructions in content.
That's data poisoning, done at training time.

checks.q: Your boss appears on a video call asking for an urgent payment. What's the safe move?
options: Verify through a separate channel you already trust
Ask them to switch the camera on
Pay: you can see their face
checks.why: Faces and voices can be cloned. Check payment requests out-of-band, even on video.
notes: The chat belongs to the same call, which might be fake.
The camera is already on. Faces and voices can be faked.
Seeing a face no longer proves who someone is.

checks.q: Why should an AI agent get only the access it needs?
options: If prompt injection tricks it, the damage it can do is limited
checks.why: Agents can be tricked by instructions hidden in what they read. Least access, plus approval for risky actions, limits the harm.
notes: Cost isn't the reason. Think about what happens if it's tricked.
Fewer permissions don't make it faster.
Agents act through the access they're given.

concept.why: AI shifts both attack and defence. Here is what is new on each side.
concept.title: How AI changes the game

items.label: Phishing at scale
items.text: Flawless, personalised lures in any language, written in seconds instead of hours.

items.label: Deepfakes
items.text: Cloned voices and video used to impersonate a boss or a family member for fraud.

items.label: Prompt injection
items.text: Hidden instructions in data trick an AI assistant into leaking or acting against its user.

items.label: Defensive AI
items.text: The other side: models that spot anomalies and triage alerts faster than people can.

keys.label: Attackers use it
keys.text: Convincing phishing, cloned voices, faster bug hunting.

keys.label: AI can be tricked
keys.text: Hidden instructions make it do what its user didn't want.

keys.label: Defenders use it
keys.text: Sorting alerts and spotting anomalies faster.

job.text: A cloud security engineer reviews who can do what, hunts for public buckets and old keys, and builds guardrails so a mistake can't reach production.

explainer.why: One key leaks eventually. See why giving each key only the access it needs stops that single leak from turning into a full breach.

title: Cloud security
hook: Most cloud breaches are misconfigurations, not clever hacks.
what: In the cloud, the provider secures the infrastructure but you secure what you put on it: the shared responsibility model. The biggest risks are storage buckets left public, over-powered access keys, leaked secrets in code, and identities with far more permissions than they need. Because everything is an API, one stolen key can be as bad as a stolen server room.

example.title: Capital One
example.text: A misconfigured web firewall let an attacker use server-side request forgery (SSRF) to grab cloud credentials from AWS's metadata service, then download data on about 100 million customers.

source.label: US Department of Justice: arrest in the Capital One data theft

defend: Least-privilege IAM roles and no long-lived keys
Block public access to storage by default
Scan code repositories for leaked secrets
Enable cloud audit logs and alerts (CloudTrail, Azure Monitor)

practice.label: Play flAWS, an AWS mistakes game

checks.q: Under the shared responsibility model, who secures your S3 bucket permissions?
checks.why: The provider secures the platform; configuration is on you.
notes: Amazon secures the platform. Bucket settings are configured by the customer.
Someone always owns it. Read the shared responsibility split.
Your internet provider has nothing to do with cloud storage settings.

checks.q: Which is one of the most common causes of cloud data leaks?
options: Storage buckets left open to the public
checks.why: Most cloud breaches come from customer misconfiguration, such as public buckets and over-powered keys, not the provider.
notes: Slow connections don't expose data.
Provider breaches are rare. Most leaks are configuration.
Two-factor authentication helps; it doesn't leak data.

checks.q: Why is a leaked cloud access key so dangerous?
options: Keys expire the moment they leak
Everything in the cloud is an API, so the key can control resources directly
It only reveals your IP address
checks.why: With the right key, an attacker can create, read or delete resources from anywhere, as if they owned the account.
notes: Leaked keys keep working until someone revokes them.
A key can do far more than run up bills.
A key grants access to resources, not just an IP address.

checks.q: A developer pushed a cloud access key to a public code repository an hour ago. What do you do first?
options: Revoke the key, issue a new one, and check what the old key was used for
Delete the commit and carry on
Wait to see if anyone uses it
checks.why: Bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Assume it's been copied: revoke it, replace it, then check the logs for what it did.
notes: Deleting the commit doesn't stop anyone who already copied the key.
Copies may already exist. The key itself is the problem.
Automated scanners find keys within minutes. Waiting gives them time.

concept.why: Most cloud incidents trace to a few mistakes. Here is where things go wrong.
concept.title: Where cloud goes wrong

items.label: Shared responsibility
items.text: The provider secures the hardware and platform; you secure your config, data and access.

items.label: Misconfiguration

title: Passwords, MFA & passkeys
hook: Identity is the new perimeter.
what: Attackers would rather log in than break in. Passwords get phished, guessed, reused and leaked. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof, but not all MFA is equal: SMS codes can be SIM-swapped, push prompts can be spammed until someone taps Approve (MFA fatigue), and fake login pages can relay codes in real time. Passkeys and hardware security keys are phishing-resistant because they only work on the real website.

example.title: Change Healthcare
example.text: Attackers used stolen credentials on a remote access portal that didn't have MFA. The ransomware attack disrupted pharmacy and insurance payments across the US for weeks.

source.label: US Senate Finance Committee hearing on the Change Healthcare attack

defend: A password manager with unique passwords everywhere
Passkeys or security keys for important accounts
Number-matching on push MFA to stop fatigue attacks
Alerts on impossible travel and new device logins

practice.label: See which sites support 2FA

checks.q: Why are passkeys considered phishing-resistant?
options: They're tied to the real website's domain and can't be used on a fake one
checks.why: The browser won't release a passkey to a look-alike domain.
notes: Length isn't what stops phishing.
That describes one-time codes. Passkeys work differently.
Biometrics unlock the passkey on your device; that isn't what makes it phishing-resistant.

checks.q: An attacker sends push MFA prompts over and over until someone taps Approve. What's this called, and what stops it?
options: MFA fatigue; number matching on push prompts
checks.why: MFA fatigue wears people down with prompts. Number matching means approving needs a code from the real login screen.
notes: Credential stuffing reuses leaked passwords, and a VPN doesn't stop prompts.
The attacker already has the password. Longer ones don't stop the prompts.
Brute force guesses passwords. Here the password is known; the target is the approval.

checks.q: Why are SMS codes weaker than other kinds of MFA?
options: An attacker can take over the phone number with a SIM swap
checks.why: SMS codes can be SIM-swapped or relayed by fake login pages. Passkeys and security keys resist both.
notes: Length isn't the weakness.
SMS codes do expire quickly.
Text messages aren't end-to-end encrypted, and that isn't the main problem.

diagram.why: Location is only a clue: an attacker with a stolen password can use a VPN to look like a normal UK sign-in. Step through a login to see where MFA stops them anyway.

steps.text: The password was leaked in a breach or captured by phishing.
The service sends a push prompt, or asks for a code or passkey, to the real owner's device.
The owner wasn't signing in, so they ignore or deny the request.
steps.stop: Number matching stops 'just tap Approve' fatigue attacks.

steps.text: Without the second factor, the password alone gets the attacker nowhere.
steps.stop: Passkeys go further: they only work on the real site, so a fake page gets nothing to replay.

approved.text: Worn down by repeated prompts, or thinking it's a glitch, the owner taps Approve. This is MFA fatigue.
approved.stop: Number matching: the phone asks for the number shown on the sign-in screen, which only the person signing in can see.

approved.text: The attacker is now signed in as the owner. Both factors were passed, so nothing looks wrong to the service.
approved.stop: Passkeys or a security key leave nothing to approve by mistake, and only work on the real site.

tip: MFA = something you know (password) + something you have (phone or key) + something you are (fingerprint). A passkey swaps the password for a private key your device keeps, so there's nothing to phish.

title: IoT & industrial systems
hook: When hacking moves from data to the physical world.
what: IoT means internet-connected devices: cameras, routers, smart TVs. OT (operational technology) and ICS (industrial control systems) run power grids, water plants and factories. These devices often run old software, rarely get patched and were built before anyone expected them to be online. Attacks here can cause physical damage, not just data loss.

example.title: Stuxnet
example.text: A highly sophisticated worm, widely attributed to the US and Israel, sabotaged Iranian uranium centrifuges by changing their speeds while showing operators normal readings. It crossed air-gapped networks via USB drives.

source.label: Symantec: W32.Stuxnet Dossier

defend: Keep industrial networks separate from office IT
Never expose control systems directly to the internet
Change default credentials and update firmware
Monitor for unexpected commands to controllers

practice.label: Read CISA's ICS advisories

checks.q: Why are OT systems hard to patch?
options: Downtime can stop a factory or utility, and devices may run for decades
checks.why: Availability and safety come first in OT, so changes are planned carefully.
notes: OT systems run software and firmware like anything else.
Patching is legal. The challenge is downtime and safety.
Many are connected, which is part of the risk.

checks.q: What does OT stand for?
checks.why: OT is the technology that runs physical processes: power grids, water plants and factories.
notes: Not about telemetry. Think about physical processes.
It's a whole category of technology, not online tools.
Nothing to do with wireless updates.

checks.q: What's the most important rule for industrial control systems?
options: Connect them to the office Wi-Fi
Never expose them directly to the internet
checks.why: Control systems were often built before anyone expected them online. Keep them off the internet and separate from office IT.
notes: Restarting a control system hourly would stop production.
Broad admin access is the opposite of safe.
The office network is exactly what should be kept separate.

checks.q: A scan finds a factory's PLC reachable from an office PC, and its patch can only go on in August. What do you do now?
options: Segment the network so only the HMI can reach the PLC, and monitor it
checks.why: In OT, uptime and safety come first, so you reduce exposure with segmentation and monitoring until the planned window.
notes: An unplanned patch can stop production or affect safety.
Unplugging stops the factory.
Leaving it reachable from the office for months is a big risk when there's a safer step.

job.text: A pentester proves the injection safely and writes up the fix (parameterised queries); a SOC analyst spots the probing in web logs and checks whether data left.

explainer.why: Here is the heart of it. Watch a normal login turn against its own database when the input is treated as code instead of data.

title: SQL injection
hook: Talk to the database directly through a login box.
what: Websites store data in databases and ask for it using SQL queries. If a site pastes your input straight into a query, you can change what the query does. Typing ' OR '1'='1 into a login box might turn 'find this user with this password' into 'find any user at all'. It's one of the oldest web bugs and it still causes major breaches.

example.title: MOVEit Transfer
example.text: A SQL injection flaw in this widely used file-transfer product let the Cl0p gang steal data from thousands of organisations in one campaign.

source.label: CISA and FBI advisory AA23-158A: CL0P exploits MOVEit

defend: Parameterised queries (prepared statements), always
Least-privilege database accounts
Input validation as a second layer
A web application firewall (WAF) as a safety net

practice.label: PortSwigger SQL injection labs (free)

checks.q: What's the real fix for SQL injection?
checks.why: Parameters keep data and code separate, so input can never become part of the query.
notes: Attackers get round blocked characters with encodings and other tricks, and real names like O'Brien need quotes.
Without errors an attacker can still ask true or false questions. The query itself must change.
HTTPS protects data in transit; the injected text still reaches the query.

checks.q: Why does ' OR '1'='1 work against a vulnerable login form?
options: It makes the query's condition always true, so it matches any user
checks.why: The input closes the quote and adds OR '1'='1, which is always true, so the query returns users without a valid password.
notes: Nothing is deleted. Look at what the extra OR does to the condition.
It doesn't encrypt anything. It changes the query's logic.
It doesn't need the password at all. That's the point.

checks.q: What does a least-privilege database account limit?
options: How much damage a successful injection can do
How many users can sign up
checks.why: If the website's database account can only read what it needs, an injection can't drop tables or read everything.
notes: Permissions don't change query speed.
Database permissions don't control who visits the site.
Sign-ups aren't limited by the database account's rights.

checks.q: A developer says: 'We hide database errors, so SQL injection can't hurt us.' What do you tell them?
options: Hidden errors only slow attackers down; use parameterised queries
Agree: without errors, attackers are blind
Add a CAPTCHA to the login form
Move the database to a different server
checks.why: Blind injection works without any error messages, by asking true or false questions. Only keeping data and code separate fixes it.
notes: Attackers can still learn from what the page shows or how long it takes. That's blind SQL injection.
A CAPTCHA slows bots on one form but doesn't stop injected text reaching the query.
Moving the database doesn't change how the app builds its queries.

keys.text: Websites ask their database for data in SQL.

keys.label: Input becomes code
keys.text: Pasting input into a query lets attackers rewrite it.

keys.label: The fix
keys.text: Parameterised queries keep input as data.

job.text: A pentester finds where user input is shown without encoding and shows the impact; developers fix it and the SOC watches for stolen sessions being reused.

explainer.why: See the difference one step makes: the same review shown escaped, then raw, and how the raw version runs in every visitor's browser.

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
hook: Make someone else's browser run your code.
what: XSS happens when a website shows user-supplied content without making it safe, so a script the attacker wrote runs in other visitors' browsers. Because it runs on the real site, it can read what the user sees, act as them and steal session tokens. Stored XSS is saved on the site (like a comment); reflected XSS bounces off a link the victim clicks.

example.title: The Samy worm
example.text: A MySpace user hid a script in his profile that added him as a friend and copied itself to the profile of anyone who viewed it. Over a million people were infected in under a day.

source.label: Samy Kamkar's own write-up of the MySpace worm

defend: Encode output for where it appears (HTML, attributes, JavaScript)
Use frameworks that escape by default
A strict Content Security Policy
HttpOnly cookies so scripts can't read sessions

practice.label: PortSwigger XSS labs (free)

checks.q: Where does an XSS payload actually run?
checks.why: That's why it can act as the victim on the trusted site.
notes: The server stores or reflects it, but the script runs somewhere else.
The database only stores it. Think about who opens the page.
The attacker plants it; it runs for the victim.

checks.q: What's the difference between stored and reflected XSS?
options: Stored targets servers; reflected targets databases
Stored is saved on the site; reflected bounces off a link the victim clicks
checks.why: A stored payload sits on the site, like a comment, and hits every visitor; a reflected one comes from a crafted link.
notes: They differ in where the script lives.
Neither is about servers or databases as targets; both run in a browser.
Both work on any browser, including phones.

checks.q: Which cookie setting stops a script from reading the session cookie?
checks.why: HttpOnly cookies are sent to the server but can't be read by JavaScript, so an XSS script can't steal them.
notes: The password isn't the issue; the session cookie is what's stolen.
HTTPS protects the cookie on the network, not from a script on the page.
Images aren't involved in reading cookies.

checks.q: Customer reviews on a shop are shown on the page exactly as typed. What should the developers do?
options: Encode user content when it's shown, and set HttpOnly on the session cookie
Only let logged-in customers post reviews
Move reviews to a separate page
checks.why: Encoding makes typed code show as text instead of running, and HttpOnly stops scripts reading the session cookie. Together they stop stored XSS stealing sessions.
notes: Logged-in customers can still post a script.
Attackers get round word filters easily, with event handlers or different spellings.
The script still runs wherever the reviews are shown.

keys.text: Hidden in a comment, a profile or a link.

keys.label: Runs for others
keys.text: The site shows it unsafely to other visitors.
