keys.text: So it can read pages and steal sessions.

job.text: A pentester changes an ID in a request to test whether the app checks ownership; engineers add the server-side check to every record.

explainer.why: See it happen. Changing one order number in the address opens another customer's data, because the server never checks whose record it is.

title: Broken access control & IDOR
hook: Change one number in the URL and see someone else's data.
what: Access control decides who can see and do what. It's #1 on the OWASP Top 10 because it's easy to get wrong. The classic version is IDOR (insecure direct object reference): /invoice/1001 is yours, and changing it to /invoice/1002 shows a stranger's because the app never checks ownership. Others include normal users reaching admin pages or APIs that trust whatever role the browser claims.

example.title: Optus
example.text: Australia's second-largest telco lost personal data on almost 10 million current and former customers. It was widely reported that an internet-facing API needed no login and used sequential customer IDs, though Optus disputed how simple the attack was.

source.label: OAIC: civil penalty action against Optus

defend: Check permissions on the server for every request
Deny by default
Use unpredictable IDs (but never rely on that alone)
Test with two accounts: can user A see user B's things?

practice.label: PortSwigger access control labs (free)

checks.q: Using random IDs instead of 1001, 1002 fully fixes IDOR. True or false?
checks.why: It makes guessing harder, but the real fix is checking ownership on every request.
notes: Random IDs make guessing harder, but anyone with a leaked ID still gets in without a check.

checks.q: Changing /invoice/1001 to /invoice/1002 shows a stranger's invoice. What's the bug?
options: IDOR: the server never checks who owns the record
checks.why: This is an insecure direct object reference: the app trusts the ID in the URL instead of checking ownership.
notes: A DDoS overwhelms a service; here one request shows the wrong data.
Nothing is injected into a query. The ID itself is simply trusted.
No script runs. The server hands over someone else's record.

checks.q: Where must permission checks happen?
options: On the server, for every request
checks.why: Anything in the browser is under the user's control. Only the server can be trusted to decide who sees what.
notes: Checking only at login lets anyone logged in see everything.
Users can change browser code, so it can't be trusted.
URLs are typed by the user. They can't enforce anything.

job.text: IT support traces why a laptop can't reach a server; a SOC analyst reads addresses, ports and protocols in every alert to know what they're looking at.

title: Networking basics
hook: IP addresses, ports, DNS: the map every attacker and defender uses.
what: Every device on a network has an IP address, its street address. Ports are the doors on that address: web traffic uses 443 (HTTPS), remote shells use 22 (SSH), Windows remote desktop uses 3389. DNS is the internet's phone book, turning names like example.com into IPs. TCP sets up a reliable conversation with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK); UDP just fires packets off. Firewalls decide which doors stay open.

example.title: Exposed RDP
example.text: Remote Desktop (port 3389) left open to the internet with weak passwords is one of ransomware gangs' favourite ways in. Sophos found RDP abused in 90% of the attacks it investigated in 2023.

source.label: Sophos: RDP abused in 90% of attacks (2024)

defend: Close every port you don't need
Put remote access behind a VPN or zero-trust gateway with MFA
Segment networks
Monitor DNS. Malware has to phone home somehow.

practice.label: Open real packet captures in Wireshark

checks.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
checks.why: 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS, 3389 is RDP.
notes: 22 is SSH, for remote admin logins.
53 is DNS, for name lookups.
3389 is Remote Desktop.

checks.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns names like example.com into IP addresses
checks.why: DNS is the internet's phone book: your device asks it for the IP address behind a name.
notes: DNS doesn't block anything by default. It answers lookups.
Encryption is done by TLS, not DNS.
MAC addresses are burned into network cards, not handed out by DNS.

checks.q: What are the three steps of a TCP handshake?
checks.why: TCP opens a reliable conversation with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge is DHCP.)
notes: That isn't a real protocol exchange.
That's DHCP, which hands out IP addresses.
Those are HTTP methods, used after a connection is open.

checks.q: A colleague can open websites by IP address but not by name. Which service should you check first?
checks.why: If addresses work but names don't, the connection is fine and the name lookup is failing. That's DNS.
notes: DHCP gave them an address already, or IP addresses wouldn't work.
Sites load fine by IP address, so the web servers are working.
The cable is fine: traffic flows when you use an IP address.

steps.text: DNS gave your PC (10.0.0.5) the website's address, 203.0.113.10, on another network. So the PC sends it to its default gateway, the router at 10.0.0.1: the frame is addressed to the router's MAC, while the packet inside still says 203.0.113.10.
The switch looks up the frame's destination MAC in its MAC address table and sends it out of the router's port only.

The router's NAT table remembers your connection, so it swaps 198.51.100.20 back to 10.0.0.5 and the switch delivers the reply to your PC.

job.text: IT support plans channels, sets up WPA3 or 802.1X and finds rogue access points; the SOC investigates when a staff network appears somewhere it shouldn't.

title: Wi-Fi & wireless security
hook: Bands, channels and the locks on the air.
what: Wi-Fi sends data by radio, so anyone in range can pick it up: encryption is what keeps it private. Networks are named by an SSID, and each access point radio has its own BSSID (a MAC address). Wi-Fi uses three bands. 2.4 GHz reaches furthest but is crowded, with only three channels that don't overlap (1, 6 and 11). 5 GHz has many more channels and more speed over a shorter range, and 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7) adds more room still. Standards have generation names: 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4, 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5 and 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6. For security, WEP is broken and must never be used. WPA2-Personal uses one shared password, so a captured handshake can be attacked offline with password guesses. WPA3-Personal uses SAE, which stops that offline guessing. Enterprise mode (802.1X with a RADIUS server) gives every user their own login, which is what businesses should use. An open network, even one with a captive portal sign-in page, doesn't encrypt anything.

example.title: KRACK
example.text: Researcher Mathy Vanhoef showed that WPA2's handshake could be tricked into reusing encryption keys (key reinstallation attacks), letting someone in range decrypt some traffic. It was a flaw in the standard itself, so it affected almost every Wi-Fi device; vendors patched it, and WPA3 was designed partly in response.

source.label: KRACK Attacks: the researchers' site

defend: Use WPA3, or WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode for older devices; never WEP
Use Enterprise mode (802.1X) for staff, so each person has their own login
Keep guests on their own network, separated from staff systems
Turn off WPS, and watch for rogue access points copying your network's name

practice.label: Read a real Wi-Fi survey in the wireless lab

checks.q: Which 2.4 GHz channels don't overlap with each other?
checks.why: Each 2.4 GHz channel is 20 MHz wide but only 5 MHz apart, so only 1, 6 and 11 avoid each other.
notes: Channels 1, 2 and 3 sit almost on top of each other.
6, 7 and 8 overlap heavily.
In 2.4 GHz three channels can sit side by side without overlapping.

checks.q: Why is WPA3-Personal stronger than WPA2-Personal?
options: Its SAE handshake stops attackers guessing the password offline from a captured handshake
checks.why: With WPA2-Personal, a captured handshake can be attacked with guesses offline. SAE means each guess needs a live exchange with the network.
notes: Password length is up to you on either. WPA3's gain is in the handshake.
Hiding the name protects nothing; it's still easy to find.
WPA3 works on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.

checks.q: Why did KRACK affect almost every Wi-Fi device?
options: It was a flaw in the WPA2 standard itself, not one vendor's code
All routers ran the same software
checks.why: When the flaw is in the standard, every correct implementation inherits it until patched.
notes: Passwords had nothing to do with it.
Different vendors' software was all affected, so it wasn't one codebase.
It affected WPA2-protected networks, not just open ones.

checks.q: A Wi-Fi survey finds an open network with your company's staff name, on hardware you don't own, in the car park. What is it most likely?
options: An evil twin trying to catch staff devices
checks.why: An open copy of your staff network name on foreign hardware is an evil twin: devices that auto-join could send traffic through the attacker.

A neighbour would use their own name, not yours.

job.text: IT support and network teams keep the network running: watching baselines, making changes through change control, and restoring service within agreed targets when things fail.

title: Running a network
hook: Racks, power, changes, monitoring and the plan for the worst day.
what: Keeping a network running is mostly careful routine, and much of it is on the exam. Physically, equipment sits in racks measured in rack units (1U is 1.75 inches, 44.45 mm). A UPS (a battery unit) rides through short power cuts and gives a generator time to start, and PDUs share power out to each device. Hot and cold aisles keep air moving, and temperature, humidity and fire suppression are watched. Processes keep it known: change management means every change is requested, assessed, approved, scheduled and recorded, with a way to roll it back. Documentation covers physical and logical diagrams, IP address records and an asset inventory, and life-cycle tracking flags kit reaching end of life or end of support. For monitoring, SNMP lets a monitoring server poll devices and receive traps (alerts); use SNMPv3, which adds authentication and encryption. Flow data such as NetFlow shows who talked to whom, syslog gathers logs, and a baseline shows what normal looks like. For disaster recovery, the RPO is how much data you can afford to lose and the RTO is how long you can afford to be down. MTBF is the average time between failures, and MTTR the average time to repair. A hot site can take over at once, a warm site has hardware but needs data and setup, and a cold site is space and power only. Plans are tested, often with a tabletop exercise.

example.title: British Airways data centre outage
example.text: On a bank holiday weekend in May 2017, British Airways lost its UK data centre. Hundreds of flights were cancelled and about 75,000 passengers were affected.

Put critical kit on a UPS, and test the generator and failover rather than just owning them
Use SNMPv3 rather than v1 or v2c, and record a baseline so you can spot what isn't normal
Agree an RPO and RTO for each system, and prove backups work by restoring them

job.text: Engineers run dual-stack IPv6, software-defined networks and zero trust access, so getting the basics right in these is part of everyday network and cloud work.

title: Modern networks: IPv6, SDN and zero trust
hook: IPv6, software-defined networks, zero trust and SASE, without the buzzwords.

explainer.why: Old networks trusted anyone inside the walls. Compare that with zero trust, which checks every request on its own, wherever it comes from.

what: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out; NAT stretched them. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, such as 2001:db8:4a1:10::25. Leading zeros can be dropped, and :: replaces one run of all-zero groups. Every IPv6 interface has a link-local address starting fe80, which only works on its own segment, and most get a global address too, often set up automatically with SLAAC. There are so many addresses that NAT isn't needed, though a firewall still decides what gets in. While both versions are in use, devices run dual stack (IPv4 and IPv6 side by side), and tunnelling or NAT64 joins IPv6-only and IPv4-only networks. Software-defined networking (SDN) splits the control plane (deciding where traffic goes) from the data plane (forwarding it), so one controller programs many devices. SD-WAN applies that to links between sites, choosing the best of several internet connections for each application. VXLAN carries layer 2 networks over layer 3, with about 16 million segment IDs instead of 4,094 VLANs. Zero trust drops the idea of a trusted inside network: every request is checked (who, which device, is it healthy) and given the least access needed. SASE delivers networking and security (secure web gateway, cloud access security broker, zero trust network access, firewall) as a cloud service close to the user. Infrastructure as code (IaC) keeps device and cloud settings as version-controlled files, so changes are reviewed and repeatable.

example.title: Google's BeyondCorp
example.text: Google moved its staff off a privileged internal network: instead of trusting anyone on the office network, every request to an internal app is checked against who the user is and the state of their device, wherever they are. Its 2014 paper said perimeter firewalls fail once an attacker is inside, and that mobile and cloud work makes a perimeter hard to hold. It became a model for zero trust.

source.label: Google Research: BeyondCorp, a new approach to enterprise security

defend: Give every user and device its own identity, and check it on every request, not just at the edge
Grant the least access needed, to each application rather than the whole network
Firewall IPv6 as carefully as IPv4: no NAT doesn't mean no filtering
Keep network and cloud settings as code, so every change is reviewed and can be rolled back

practice.label: Read a PC's IPv6 addresses in the IPv6 lab

notes: You can't drop the zeros at the end of a group, and :: means a run of zero groups.
:: can appear only once in an address.
Leading zeros can go, but '2001' has none to drop.

Separating guests from staff is a VLAN or policy job.

checks.why: Zero trust checks each request on its own merits, so being on the network grants nothing.
notes: Address space wasn't the reason.

SD-WAN connects sites; it's not why Google dropped the trusted inside.

job.text: Engineers choose the right algorithm, keep keys out of code and in a vault, and check that passwords are stored with a slow, salted hash.

explainer.why: See a hash in action. The same input always gives the same fingerprint, one small change rewrites it completely, and that is why passwords are hashed, not stored.

title: Encryption & hashing
hook: Locks, keys and fingerprints for data.
what: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Symmetric encryption (AES) uses one shared key. Asymmetric encryption (RSA, elliptic curve) uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock, which is how HTTPS starts a secure connection with a site you've never met. Hashing is different: it's a one-way fingerprint. You can't reverse it, so sites store password hashes, ideally with slow algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2 plus a unique salt.

example.title: LinkedIn
example.text: In 2012 about 6.5 million LinkedIn password hashes were posted online; in 2016 it emerged the same breach covered about 117 million accounts. The hashes used SHA-1 with no salt, so attackers cracked most of them quickly with precomputed tables.

source.label: Troy Hunt: Observations on the LinkedIn data breach

defend: Use TLS everywhere
Hash passwords with bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 and a salt
Never write your own crypto; use vetted libraries
Protect and rotate keys (key management is the hard part)

practice.label: Learn by breaking crypto on CryptoHack

checks.q: Why do sites hash passwords instead of encrypting them?
options: Hashes can't be turned back into the password, so a leak reveals less
checks.why: The site only needs to check a match, never read the original.
notes: Hashes aren't meant to be reversed at all.
Encrypting passwords is legal; it's just the wrong tool.
Length isn't the point; it's one-way versus reversible.

checks.q: Which kind of encryption uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock?
options: Asymmetric, such as RSA or elliptic curve
checks.why: Asymmetric encryption is how HTTPS starts a secure connection with a site you've never met. Then both sides switch to a fast shared key.
notes: Symmetric uses the same key to lock and unlock.
Hashing is one-way; there's nothing to unlock.
Base64 is encoding with no key at all.

checks.q: Why should each password hash use a unique salt?
options: So the hash can be reversed later
So identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work
checks.why: A salt is random data added before hashing, so attackers can't crack many identical passwords at once with ready-made tables.
notes: Salts don't make hashes reversible.
A salt is added per password, not used to encrypt the database.
A salt doesn't shorten the hash.

checks.q: A developer stores passwords as unsalted MD5 'because it's hashed'. What do you recommend?
options: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2
Encrypt the MD5 hashes with AES
Keep MD5 but make passwords longer
checks.why: Password hashes need to be slow and salted, so leaked hashes are expensive to crack one by one. MD5 is fast and, unsalted, falls to precomputed tables.
notes: Encrypting the hashes adds a key to protect, and the hashes underneath are still fast to crack.
Base64 is encoding: anyone can reverse it.
Longer passwords help, but MD5 is still fast to guess against.

steps.text: Your browser starts a TLS connection and offers the encryption methods it supports.
The server sends a certificate signed by a trusted authority, so you know it's the real site.
Both sides work out the same secret key using public-key maths, without ever sending the key itself. (This is TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 does the same exchange inside the two hellos.)
Everything after that, such as your password and balance, is encrypted with the shared key. The eavesdropper only sees scrambled bytes.
steps.stop: Use TLS everywhere, and never click through certificate warnings.

tip: Encryption is two-way, hashing is one-way. You unlock an encrypted file with the key; you can't un-blend a hash back to the original; you can only check whether two things hash the same.

job.text: Someone has to renew certificates before they expire, fix the chain when a browser complains, and automate it so it doesn't happen again.

title: Certificates & PKI
hook: How your browser knows a site is real.

explainer.why: See what your browser checks before it trusts a site: the right name, a valid date, and a signature it recognises. Break each one and watch what happens.

what: A certificate ties a public key to a name, like shop.example.com. A certificate authority (CA) checks that the requester controls the name, then signs the certificate. Your device trusts a short list of root CAs, built into the operating system or browser. Roots sign intermediate CAs, which sign site certificates, so your browser follows the chain up to a root it already trusts. To get a certificate, a server sends the CA a certificate signing request (CSR) holding its public key; the private key never leaves the server. If that key is stolen, the certificate is revoked: CAs publish revocation lists (CRLs) and can answer single questions over OCSP, though many browsers now get revocation data pushed to them by the browser maker instead. This whole system of CAs, certificates and trust is called PKI.

example.title: DigiNotar
example.text: Attackers broke into DigiNotar, a Dutch certificate authority, and issued themselves a valid certificate for google.com. It was used to intercept Gmail traffic, mostly from users in Iran. Browser makers removed DigiNotar from their trusted lists, which made every certificate it had issued worthless, and the company went bankrupt within weeks.

source.label: Fox-IT interim report on DigiNotar (filed with the SEC by its parent, VASCO)

defend: Keep private keys on the server (or in a hardware security module) and never email them
Revoke and replace a certificate as soon as its key may be exposed
Automate renewal so certificates never expire unnoticed
Never click through a browser's certificate warning on a site you log in to

checks.q: What does a certificate authority do when it signs a certificate?
options: Encrypts the website's data for it
Vouches that the public key in it belongs to that name
checks.why: The CA checks the requester controls the name, then signs to say so. Your browser trusts that signature because it trusts the CA.
notes: The CA never sees the site's traffic. Its signature says something about the key.
The private key never leaves the server. The CA only sees the public key.
Signing has nothing to do with speed.

checks.q: A server's private key is stolen. What should happen to its certificate?
options: Renew it with the same key
Revoke it and issue a new one with a new key pair
checks.why: Revocation tells clients to stop trusting it, and a new key pair makes the stolen key useless for the replacement.
notes: Anyone with the stolen key can pretend to be the site until it's revoked.
Renewing with the same key leaves the thief able to use it.
The password isn't the problem; the stolen private key is.

checks.q: Why did removing DigiNotar from browsers' trusted lists stop its rogue google.com certificate working?
options: Browsers check every certificate's chain up to a trusted root
checks.why: No trusted root means no trusted chain, so every DigiNotar certificate failed the check.
notes: Changing addresses doesn't affect a certificate the browser already trusts.
Certificates are public. Trust comes from the chain.
Gmail kept using HTTPS. The browsers removed trust in the CA.

checks.q: Staff see a certificate warning on the internal printer's admin page, which uses a self-signed certificate. What's the sensible fix?
options: Issue it a certificate from the company's internal CA, trusted on staff devices
Tell staff to always click 'Proceed anyway'
Turn off HTTPS on the printer
Buy a public certificate for the printer's internal address
checks.why: An internal CA gives internal devices trusted certificates. Teaching people to click through warnings trains them to ignore real ones.
notes: Clicking through warnings becomes a habit attackers can exploit on real sites.
That sends the admin password in clear text across the network.
Public CAs don't issue certificates for internal-only names or private addresses.

job.text: Most servers run Linux. IT support fixes them over SSH, a SOC analyst searches their logs with grep, and a pentester works from a Linux machine all day.

title: Linux command line
hook: Most servers and most security tools live here.
what: Most of the internet runs on Linux, and most security tools are built for it. Core commands to know: ls (list files), cd (move), cat and less (read files), grep (search text), find (search files), ps and top (running processes), ss or netstat (network connections), chmod and chown (permissions), sudo (run as admin). example.title: Log triage

source.label: MITRE ATT&CK T1110.001: Password guessing

Run services as unprivileged users
Keep packages updated
Ship logs somewhere attackers can't delete them

job.text: This is the job: a queue of alerts, searching logs in the SIEM, deciding what's real, asking other teams to act, and handing over to the next shift.

title: The SOC, SIEM & logs
hook: Where most cyber careers start.
what: A Security Operations Center (SOC) is the team that watches for attacks around the clock. Logs from servers, laptops, firewalls and cloud services flow into a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) tool such as Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel or Elastic, where detection rules raise alerts. Analysts triage each alert: is it real, how bad is it, and what's affected? Most alerts are false positives, so the skill is investigating quickly and calmly.

title: Incident response

what: Incident response (IR) is the plan for when something goes wrong. The classic phases: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned. title: OSINT
hook: Finding out a lot from what's already public.
what: Open-Source Intelligence means gathering information from public sources: websites, social media, job ads, DNS records, code repositories, breach dumps and photo metadata. Attackers use it to plan phishing and find exposed systems. Defenders use it to see their organisation the way attackers do. Ethical OSINT stays on public information and respects privacy: you investigate organisations and threats, not stalk individuals.

Monitor for leaked credentials and code

job.text: A GRC analyst keeps the risk register: scores each risk, finds it an owner, agrees what to do about it, and brings it back for review when facts change.

title: Risk, simply
hook: How organisations decide which dangers to fix first, and which to live with.
what: Risk is the chance that a threat exploits a weakness, combined with how much it would hurt. Most organisations score both on a simple scale, often 1 to 5, so likelihood × impact gives a score from 1 to 25 and the biggest numbers get attention first. Each risk goes in a risk register with an owner: a named person who decides what happens to it. There are four ways to treat a risk: mitigate it (add controls so it is less likely or less harmful), transfer it (insurance or a contract), avoid it (stop doing the risky thing) or accept it (live with it, on record). Risk appetite is how much risk leadership is willing to take on; anything above it must be treated. What is left after controls is the residual risk. Some teams also put a money figure on it: single loss expectancy (SLE) × annual rate of occurrence (ARO) = annual loss expectancy (ALE). A business impact analysis (BIA) works out which systems matter most, how fast they must come back (RTO) and how much data you could afford to lose (RPO).

example.title: TSB's IT migration
example.text: TSB moved 5.2 million customers to a new banking platform in April 2018. Many were locked out for days and some saw other customers' details. In 2022 the UK regulators fined TSB £48.65 million for failing to manage the risks of the change.

source.label: FCA: TSB fined £48.65m for operational resilience failings

A risk that has been insured

notes: That's the inherent risk, before controls.

checks.why: Every risk needs a named owner with the authority to fund a fix or accept it.

Auditors check the process; they don't make the decision.

checks.why: ALE = SLE × ARO = £20,000 × 0.5 = £10,000 a year, a guide to how much a control is worth spending.
notes: That doubles the loss. ARO 0.5 means once every two years.
That's the SLE, before allowing for how often it happens.

options: It needs treating, or accepting by someone with the authority to go over appetite
Accept it: someone has signed off
checks.why: Appetite sets what can simply be accepted. Over it, the risk must be treated or accepted at the level the board has set.
notes: A signature from someone without the authority isn't real acceptance.
Changing the number doesn't change the risk.
Hiding a risk makes it worse.

items.label: Payment fraud by email
items.text: Fake bank-change emails arrive most months, and one paid invoice could cost tens of thousands.
items.treat: Mitigate: call the supplier back on a known number before any bank change.

items.label: Ransomware on the file server
items.text: Less frequent, but client files and billing would stop for days.
items.treat: Mitigate: offline backups, MFA on remote access and prompt patching.

items.label: Stolen laptop
items.text: Happens most years, but the disks are encrypted.
items.treat: Accept, on record: encryption already limits the harm.

items.label: Cloud booking system outage
items.text: Rare, but bookings stop until the supplier recovers.
items.treat: Transfer: a contract with service levels and credits.

items.label: Office flood
items.text: Unlikely, but severe if it happens.
items.treat: Transfer: insurance, plus backups kept off site.

tip: Accepting a risk is a valid choice, but only on record and signed off by its owner. An accepted risk that nobody wrote down is just a forgotten one.

job.text: GRC makes sure the company meets UK GDPR and PCI DSS; a pentester never starts without the owner's authorisation, because testing without it is an offence under the Computer Misuse Act; the written agreement proves what was allowed.

title: The law and compliance
hook: The rules that decide what you're allowed to touch, and what must happen after a breach.
what: Laws set the floor, and some apply to you as soon as you start practising. In the UK, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it an offence to access a computer without authorisation (section 1), to do so in order to commit another offence (section 2), or to impair a system, for example with malware or a denial-of-service attack (section 3). Making, supplying or obtaining a tool intending it to be used for one of these offences, or believing it's likely to be, is covered too (section 3A); simply owning a security tool isn't. Good intentions are no defence: what matters is authorisation from someone entitled to give it, which is why testers work from a signed scope. UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 cover personal data. They set seven principles, including keeping data secure (integrity and confidentiality); a notifiable breach must be reported to the ICO without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (later reports must say why); and fines can reach £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover. The NIS Regulations 2018 cover essential services such as energy and transport, and the EU's NIS2 widens this across Europe. Some rules are contracts, not laws: PCI DSS is required by the card brands of anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data. In the EU, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) covers financial firms' digital resilience. Breaking these rules can bring fines, lost contracts or licences, and lasting damage to reputation. This is a plain-English summary for learning, not legal advice.

example.title: TalkTalk
example.text: Attackers used SQL injection on old web pages to steal data on about 157,000 customers. Several were convicted under the Computer Misuse Act, and the ICO fined TalkTalk £400,000 for failing to protect the data: both sides of the law in one breach.

job.text: SOC teams map alerts to ATT&CK techniques to find detection gaps; GRC and design reviews use STRIDE to spot threats before something is built.

title: How attacks are modelled
hook: Shared maps of how attacks unfold, so defenders can spot them and break them.
what: Defenders use models to describe attacks in a shared language. The Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin, 2011) breaks an intrusion into seven stages: reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. Break any link and the attack fails, ideally early. MITRE ATT&CK is a far more detailed catalogue built from real incidents: tactics are the attacker's goals (such as initial access or persistence) and techniques are how they achieve them, each with an ID such as T1566 for phishing. The Diamond Model links four parts of every intrusion event: adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim, so one known piece helps you find the others. Threat modelling turns this round before anything is built: STRIDE asks what could go wrong with a design under six headings: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

example.title: Advisories written in ATT&CK
example.text: #StopRansomware advisories from CISA and the FBI, often with partners such as the UK NCSC, list each technique a ransomware group uses with its ATT&CK ID, so defenders everywhere can check their detections against the same list.

source.label: CISA: #StopRansomware

checks.q: In the Cyber Kill Chain, which stage comes straight after delivery?
checks.why: Delivery gets the weapon to the target (an email, a link); exploitation is when it runs and takes advantage of a weakness.
notes: Installation comes after the weapon has run.
Reconnaissance is the first stage, before delivery.

checks.q: In MITRE ATT&CK, what is a tactic?
options: The attacker's goal at that point, such as persistence
checks.why: Tactics are the 'why' (initial access, persistence, exfiltration); techniques are the 'how', each with an ID like T1566.
notes: Malware is a tool, not a tactic.

checks.q: An attacker changes the price in a request before it reaches the shop's server. Which STRIDE threat is that?
checks.why: Tampering is changing data you shouldn't be able to change. It breaks integrity.
notes: Spoofing is pretending to be someone else.
Repudiation is denying you did something.
Elevation of privilege is gaining powers you shouldn't have.

checks.q: Which four parts does the Diamond Model link?
checks.why: Every intrusion event has someone (adversary) using something (capability) over something (infrastructure) against someone (victim).
notes: That's the NIST CSF's functions.
That's a common people-process-technology model.
That's the CIA triad plus authenticity.
